run.source_title: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks

target_claim.text: Modern neural networks are substantially less well calibrated than older neural networks, while temperature scaling is often effective for calibrating their predictions.

selection_reason.why_attackable: The comparison spans different architectures and eras, and the conclusions rely primarily on empirical calibration measures across selected datasets rather than broad deployment settings.

artifact.weak_point: 시대 효과를 주장하면서 LeNet과 ResNet처럼 깊이·구조·학습 절차가 크게 다른 모델을 비교해, 관찰된 보정 차이를 ‘현대성’ 자체의 효과로 분리하지 못한다.

assumptions.text: The older and modern neural-network comparisons isolate changes associated with model era rather than confounding architecture, depth, training procedure, or dataset.
assumptions.failure_effect: The claim that modern networks are substantially less calibrated than older networks would be weakened to a comparison of particular model configurations.

assumptions.text: The calibration measures used in the experiments validly capture whether confidence estimates represent true correctness likelihood across the evaluated classification tasks.
assumptions.failure_effect: Poor measured calibration could reflect limitations of the metric or evaluation design rather than unreliable probabilities.

assumptions.text: The selected older networks and cited historical baseline are representative enough to support a broad older-versus-modern conclusion.
assumptions.failure_effect: The result could be driven by the particular LeNet and historical binary-task comparison rather than an era-wide pattern.

assumptions.text: Temperature scaling retains useful calibration performance beyond the selected state-of-the-art architectures and vision or NLP tasks evaluated in the paper.
assumptions.failure_effect: The conclusion would need to be restricted to the tested models and tasks, rather than claiming that temperature scaling is often effective generally.

attack_questions.question: How can the paper attribute the calibration gap to modernity when its illustrative comparison contrasts a 5-layer LeNet with a 110-layer ResNet, potentially changing architecture, depth, training, and task conditions simultaneously?
attack_questions.why_likely: The central historical comparison uses visibly different model families and eras, so confounding is a direct threat to the headline result.

attack_questions.question: What evidence shows that the reported calibration measures distinguish genuinely non-probabilistic confidence estimates from artifacts of the chosen confidence summaries or benchmark evaluation procedure?
attack_questions.why_likely: The claim relies on empirical calibration measures to infer whether confidence represents true correctness likelihood.

attack_questions.question: On what basis is temperature scaling described as often effective outside the selected state-of-the-art architectures and computer-vision or NLP tasks?
attack_questions.why_likely: The cited evidence describes experiments on selected tasks and architectures, while the conclusion is broader than those settings.

qualifies.rationale: The illustrative comparison uses a 5-layer LeNet and 110-layer ResNet under the same CIFAR-100 task, but the paper explicitly states that it cannot claim causality and discusses capacity and regularization as associated factors. The evidence reports ECE, MCE, NLL, and reliability diagrams, but explicitly notes that MCE is highly sensitive to binning and less suited to small test sets, leaving measurement-validity concerns. The table reports temperature-scaling results across multiple vision and NLP datasets and architectures, indicating effectiveness in several tested settings, though not broad validity beyond those experiments.

Observing Miscalibration


The architecture and training procedures of neural networks have rapidly evolved in recent years. In this section we identify some recent changes that are responsible for the miscalibration phenomenon observed in Figure 1. Though we cannot claim causality, we find that increased model capacity and lack of regularization are closely related to model miscalibration.

Model capacity. The model capacity of neural networks has increased at a dramatic pace over the past few years.

It is now common to see networks with hundreds, if not thousands of layers (He et al., 2016;Huang et al., 2016) and hundreds of convolutional filters per layer (Zagoruyko & Komodakis, 2016). Recent work shows that very deep or wide models are able to generalize better than smaller ones, while exhibiting the capacity to easily fit the training set (Zhang et al., 2017).

Although increasing depth and width may reduce classification error, we observe that these increases negatively affect model calibration. Figure 2 displays error and ECE as a function of depth and width on a ResNet trained on CIFAR-100. The far left figure varies depth for a network with 64 convolutional filters per layer, while the middle left figure fixes the depth at 14 layers and varies the number of convolutional filters per layer. Though even the smallest models in the graph exhibit some degree of miscalibration, the ECE metric grows substantially with model capacity. During training, after the model is able to correctly classify (almost) all training samples, NLL can be further minimized by increasing the confidence of predictions. Increased model capacity will lower training NLL, and thus the model will be more (over)confident on average.

TRAINING SETUP


Architectures and training configurations. We adopt two state-of-the-art neural network architectures, including DenseNet (Huang et al., 2016) and Wide ResNet (Zagoruyko & Komodakis, 2016). For DenseNet, our model follows the same setup as in (Huang et al., 2016), with depth L = 100, growth rate k = 12 (Dense-BC) and dropout rate 0. In addition, we evaluate the method on a Wide ResNet, with depth 28, width 10 (WRN-28-10) and dropout rate 0. Furthermore, in Appendix A.1, we provide additional experimental results on another Wide ResNet with depth 40, width 4 (WRN-40-4). The hyper-parameters of neural networks are set identical to the original Wide ResNet (Zagoruyko & Komodakis, 2016) and DenseNet (Huang et al., 2016) implementations. All neural networks are trained with stochastic gradient descent with Nesterov momentum (Duchi et al., 2011;Kingma & Ba, 2014). Specifically, we train Dense-BC for 300 epochs with batch size 64 and momentum 0.9; and Wide ResNet for 200 epochs with batch size 128 and momentum 0.9. The learning rate starts at 0.1, and is dropped by a factor of 10 at 50% and 75% of the training progress, respectively.

The following datasets are used in the experiments:

• CIFAR-10 [19]: The dataset consists of 60 000 color images 32 × 32. Training / validation / test splits are respectively 50 000 / 5 000 / 5 000.

unresolved.snippet:
Contributions.
This paper makes three contributions: Systematic scaling law characterization in the sub-20M regime. We measure the accuracy–model-size relationship across nearly three orders of magnitude (22K–19.8M parameters) with two architecture families on CIFAR-100. We report architecture-dependent exponents that are 1.4–2 steeper than the large-model regime, though this comparison is approximate because prior work fit to cross-entropy loss while we fit to error rate (Section ). We also document a broken power law and architecture-specific saturation. Error redistribution under width scaling. The Jaccard overlap between error sets of the smallest and largest models is only 0.35 ( across 25 seed pairs), below the 0.42 expected from pure subset containment and well above the 0.21 expected from independent errors. limitations: The paper states that it cannot claim causality for the relationships between architectural or training factors and calibration.
The experiments assume that training, validation, and test sets are drawn from the same distribution.
Finite-sample binning approximations such as ECE and reliability diagrams may not fully characterize calibration.
The provided source spans are abstracts and introductory passages, not the underlying experimental tables, metrics, datasets, or calibration protocols.

p1_b32.text: Conﬁdence calibration – the problem of predict- ing probability estimates representative of the true correctness likelihood – is important for classiﬁcation models in many applications. We discover that modern neural networks, unlike those from a decade ago, are poorly calibrated. Through extensive experiments, we observe that depth, width, weight decay, and Batch Normal- ization are important factors inﬂuencing calibra- tion. We evaluate the performance of various post-processing calibration methods on state-of- the-art architectures with image and document classiﬁcation datasets. Our analysis and exper- iments not only offer insights into neural net- work learning, but also provide a simple and straightforward recipe for practical settings: on most datasets, temperature scaling – a single- parameter variant of Platt Scaling – is surpris- ingly effective at calibrating predictions.

p2_b8.text: In 2005, Niculescu-Mizil & Caruana (2005) showed that neural networks typically produce well-calibrated proba- bilities on binary classiﬁcation tasks. While neural net- works today are undoubtedly more accurate than they were a decade ago, we discover with great surprise that mod- ern neural networks are no longer well-calibrated. This is visualized in Figure 1, which compares a 5-layer LeNet (left) (LeCun et al., 1998) with a 110-layer ResNet (right) (He et al., 2016) on the CIFAR-100 dataset. The top row shows the distribution of prediction conﬁdence (i.e. prob- abilities associated with the predicted label) as histograms. The average conﬁdence of LeNet closely matches its accu- racy, while the average conﬁdence of the ResNet is substan- tially higher than its accuracy. This is further illustrated in the bottom row reliability diagrams (DeGroot & Fienberg, 1983; Niculescu-Mizil & Caruana, 2005), which show ac- curacy as a function of conﬁdence. We see that LeNet is well-calibrated, as conﬁdence closely approximates the ex- pected accuracy (i.e. the bars align roughly along the diag- onal). On the other hand, the ResNet’s accuracy is better, but does not match its conﬁdence.

p2_b17.text: Our goal is not only to understand why neural networks have become miscalibrated, but also to identify what meth- ods can alleviate this problem. In this paper, we demon- strate on several computer vision and NLP tasks that neu- ral networks produce conﬁdences that cannot represent true probabilities. Additionally, we offer insight and intuition into network training and architectural trends that may cause miscalibration. Finally, we compare various post- processing calibration methods on state-of-the-art neural networks, and introduce several extensions of our own. Surprisingly, we ﬁnd that a single-parameter variant of Platt scaling (Platt et al., 1999) – which we refer to as temper- ature scaling – is often the most effective method at ob- taining calibrated probabilities. Because this method is straightforward to implement with existing deep learning frameworks, it can be easily adopted in practical settings.

nodes.text: Modern neural networks are substantially less well calibrated than older neural networks, while temperature scaling is often effective for calibrating their predictions.
Greater model depth and width, Batch Normalization, and reduced weight decay are associated with worse calibration, even when some of these changes improve classification accuracy.
Calibration and classification accuracy are not optimized by the same weight-decay setting; calibration can continue improving after the setting that yields optimal accuracy.
Neural networks can improve classification accuracy while overfitting NLL, producing better decisions at the expense of well-modeled probabilities and thereby contributing to miscalibration.
Across the evaluated image and document classification tasks and state-of-the-art architectures, temperature scaling is often the most effective post-processing calibration method.

obligations.question: How can the paper attribute the calibration gap to modernity when its illustrative comparison contrasts a 5-layer LeNet with a 110-layer ResNet, potentially changing architecture, depth, training, and task conditions simultaneously?

What evidence shows that the reported calibration measures distinguish genuinely non-probabilistic confidence estimates from artifacts of the chosen confidence summaries or benchmark evaluation procedure?
On what basis is temperature scaling described as often effective outside the selected state-of-the-art architectures and computer-vision or NLP tasks?

actions.rationale: Finds studies testing whether architecture and depth, rather than model era, explain calibration differences.

claims.text: Modern neural networks are substantially less well calibrated than older neural networks, while temperature scaling is often effective for calibrating their predictions.
claims.attack_rationale: The comparison spans different architectures and eras, and the conclusions rely primarily on empirical calibration measures across selected datasets rather than broad deployment settings.

claims.text: Greater model depth and width, Batch Normalization, and reduced weight decay are associated with worse calibration, even when some of these changes improve classification accuracy.
claims.attack_rationale: The paper explicitly does not claim causality, and the associations are demonstrated mainly in particular CIFAR-100 model families using ECE.

claims.text: Calibration and classification accuracy are not optimized by the same weight-decay setting; calibration can continue improving after the setting that yields optimal accuracy.
claims.attack_rationale: This relationship is reported for a 110-layer ResNet on CIFAR-100, and its interpretation depends on the chosen calibration and accuracy metrics.

claims.text: Neural networks can improve classification accuracy while overfitting NLL, producing better decisions at the expense of well-modeled probabilities and thereby contributing to miscalibration.
claims.attack_rationale: The proposed explanation is inferred from training curves and observed metric divergence, so the causal mechanism may not be uniquely established.

claims.text: Across the evaluated image and document classification tasks and state-of-the-art architectures, temperature scaling is often the most effective post-processing calibration method.
claims.attack_rationale: The claim depends on the selected calibration baselines, datasets, architectures, and validation procedures, and may not transfer to other tasks or distribution shifts.

limitations: The paper states that it cannot claim causality for the relationships between architectural or training factors and calibration.
The experiments assume that training, validation, and test sets are drawn from the same distribution.
Finite-sample binning approximations such as ECE and reliability diagrams may not fully characterize calibration.

assumptions.text: The older and modern neural-network comparisons isolate changes associated with model era rather than confounding architecture, depth, training procedure, or dataset.
assumptions.failure_effect: The claim that modern networks are substantially less calibrated than older networks would be weakened to a comparison of particular model configurations.

assumptions.text: The calibration measures used in the experiments validly capture whether confidence estimates represent true correctness likelihood across the evaluated classification tasks.
assumptions.failure_effect: Poor measured calibration could reflect limitations of the metric or evaluation design rather than unreliable probabilities.

assumptions.text: The selected older networks and cited historical baseline are representative enough to support a broad older-versus-modern conclusion.
assumptions.failure_effect: The result could be driven by the particular LeNet and historical binary-task comparison rather than an era-wide pattern.

assumptions.text: Temperature scaling retains useful calibration performance beyond the selected state-of-the-art architectures and vision or NLP tasks evaluated in the paper.
assumptions.failure_effect: The conclusion would need to be restricted to the tested models and tasks, rather than claiming that temperature scaling is often effective generally.

attack_questions.question: How can the paper attribute the calibration gap to modernity when its illustrative comparison contrasts a 5-layer LeNet with a 110-layer ResNet, potentially changing architecture, depth, training, and task conditions simultaneously?
attack_questions.why_likely: The central historical comparison uses visibly different model families and eras, so confounding is a direct threat to the headline result.

attack_questions.question: What evidence shows that the reported calibration measures distinguish genuinely non-probabilistic confidence estimates from artifacts of the chosen confidence summaries or benchmark evaluation procedure?
attack_questions.why_likely: The claim relies on empirical calibration measures to infer whether confidence represents true correctness likelihood.

attack_questions.question: On what basis is temperature scaling described as often effective outside the selected state-of-the-art architectures and computer-vision or NLP tasks?
attack_questions.why_likely: The cited evidence describes experiments on selected tasks and architectures, while the conclusion is broader than those settings.

Architectures and training configurations. We adopt two state-of-the-art neural network architectures, including DenseNet (Huang et al., 2016) and Wide ResNet (Zagoruyko & Komodakis, 2016). Specifically, we train Dense-BC for 300 epochs with batch size 64 and momentum 0.9; and Wide ResNet for 200 epochs with batch size 128 and momentum 0.9. The learning rate starts at 0.1, and is dropped by a factor of 10 at 50% and 75% of the training progress, respectively.

Experimental Design


The following datasets are used in the experiments:

• CIFAR-10 [19]: The dataset consists of 60 000 color images 32 × 32. Training / validation / test splits are respectively 50 000 / 5 000 / 5 000.

• CIFAR-100 [19]: 60 000 color images 32 × 32, 100 classes. Training / validation / test: 50 000 / 5 000 / 5 000.

• ImageNet 2012 [10]: Large dataset with color images organized into 1000 classes.

Training / validation / test: 1.2 m / 25 000 / 25 000.

• Tiny ImageNet [10]: 110 000 color images 64 × 64, organized into 200 classes, subset of the previous dataset. Training / validation / test: 100 000 / 5 000 / 5 000.

Pre-trained neural networks with various architectures from open repositories were used for calculations. In experiments, models and datasets are divided into two main groups:

1. The first group includes neural networks trained on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet.

The weights for the models are obtained respectively from the repositories [20, 21, 22]. Models from this group are used to compare calibration methods based on post-processing.

2. The second group includes pre-trained neural networks from the repository [23]. The datasets used here are CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet. These neural networks were trained in [18] -focal error and label smoothing were used for the considered models.

The models were trained on the training data (or its subset), calibrated on the validation set -all diagrams and metrics correspond to the test set.

Code used in all experiments is published in [24]: temperature, vector, and matrix scaling are implemented using PyTorch, and other methods and evaluation are implemented with SciPY and scikit-learn. Histogram binning use 20 bins; ECE, cwECE, and MCE are calculated on 15 bins partition; reliability diagrams use 10 bins.

reference_chunks.content:
Observing Miscalibration


The architecture and training procedures of neural networks have rapidly evolved in recent years. In this section we identify some recent changes that are responsible for the miscalibration phenomenon observed in Figure 1. Though we cannot claim causality, we find that increased model capacity and lack of regularization are closely related to model miscalibration.

Model capacity. The model capacity of neural networks has increased at a dramatic pace over the past few years.

It is now common to see networks with hundreds, if not thousands of layers (He et al., 2016;Huang et al., 2016) and hundreds of convolutional filters per layer (Zagoruyko & Komodakis, 2016). Recent work shows that very deep or wide models are able to generalize better than smaller ones, while exhibiting the capacity to easily fit the training set (Zhang et al., 2017).

Although increasing depth and width may reduce classification error, we observe that these increases negatively affect model calibration. Figure 2 displays error and ECE as a function of depth and width on a ResNet trained on CIFAR-100. The far left figure varies depth for a network with 64 convolutional filters per layer, while the middle left figure fixes the depth at 14 layers and varies the number of convolutional filters per layer. Though even the smallest models in the graph exhibit some degree of miscalibration, the ECE metric grows substantially with model capacity. During training, after the model is able to correctly classify (almost) all training samples, NLL can be further minimized by increasing the confidence of predictions. Increased model capacity will lower training NLL, and thus the model will be more (over)confident on average.

reference_chunks.source_title: A survey of the recent architectures of deep convolutional neural networks

reference_chunks.content:
Experimental Design


The following datasets are used in the experiments:

• CIFAR-10 [19]: The dataset consists of 60 000 color images 32 × 32. Training / validation / test splits are respectively 50 000 / 5 000 / 5 000.

• CIFAR-100 [19]: 60 000 color images 32 × 32, 100 classes. Training / validation / test: 50 000 / 5 000 / 5 000.

• ImageNet 2012 [10]: Large dataset with color images organized into 1000 classes.

Training / validation / test: 1.2 m / 25 000 / 25 000.

• Tiny ImageNet [10]: 110 000 color images 64 × 64, organized into 200 classes, subset of the previous dataset. Training / validation / test: 100 000 / 5 000 / 5 000.

Pre-trained neural networks with various architectures from open repositories were used for calculations. In experiments, models and datasets are divided into two main groups:

1. The first group includes neural networks trained on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet.

The weights for the models are obtained respectively from the repositories [20, 21, 22]. Models from this group are used to compare calibration methods based on post-processing.

2. The second group includes pre-trained neural networks from the repository [23]. The datasets used here are CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet. These neural networks were trained in [18] -focal error and label smoothing were used for the considered models.

The models were trained on the training data (or its subset), calibrated on the validation set -all diagrams and metrics correspond to the test set.

Code used in all experiments is published in [24]: temperature, vector, and matrix scaling are implemented using PyTorch, and other methods and evaluation are implemented with SciPY and scikit-learn. Histogram binning use 20 bins; ECE, cwECE, and MCE are calculated on 15 bins partition; reliability diagrams use 10 bins.

Contributions.
This paper makes three contributions: Systematic scaling law characterization in the sub-20M regime. We measure the accuracy–model-size relationship across nearly three orders of magnitude (22K–19.8M parameters) with two architecture families on CIFAR-100. We report architecture-dependent exponents that are 1.4–2 steeper than the large-model regime, though this comparison is approximate because prior work fit to cross-entropy loss while we fit to error rate (Section ). We also document a broken power law and architecture-specific saturation. Error redistribution under width scaling. The Jaccard overlap between error sets of the smallest and largest models is only 0.35 ( across 25 seed pairs), below the 0.42 expected from pure subset containment and well above the 0.21 expected from independent errors. Compression changes which inputs are misclassified, not merely how many. Class triage and calibration inversion. Small models develop extreme triage strategies (Gini coefficient of per-class accuracy: 0.26 at 22K parameters vs. 0.09 at 4.7M), and the smallest models are the best calibrated, with ECE following an inverted-U pattern in ScaleCNN—contrary to the usual assumption that overconfidence grows monotonically with capacity.
reference_chunks.source_title: Scaling Laws in the Tiny Regime: How Small Models Change Their Mistakes

reference_chunks.content:
Future Work
The most pressing next step is replicating these experiments across additional datasets and architectures. CIFAR-10 (fewer classes), Tiny ImageNet (200 classes, 6464, more training data), and Speech Commands v2 (audio, a standard TinyML benchmark) would test whether the scaling exponents and error redistribution patterns we observe are specific to CIFAR-100 or reflect something more general about the small-model regime. Similarly, extending to EfficientNet-Lite, tiny vision transformers, and NAS-derived architectures would clarify whether the architecture-dependence finding holds broadly. With denser sampling of model sizes, it would also be possible to do proper model selection (AIC/BIC) to distinguish between a power law, a broken power law, and other candidate functional forms. A second line of work would test whether the error redistribution pattern generalizes beyond width scaling. Applying structured pruning and post-training quantization to the trained models from this study would reveal whether all forms of capacity reduction produce the same kind of error rearrangement, or whether width scaling is a special case. Evaluating the same models on CIFAR-100-C [hendrycks2019benchmarking] would test whether robustness degrades smoothly or shows sharper collapses at particular model sizes. Finally, while we have measured from the CIFAR-100 eigenspectrum, directly measuring from the effective rank of trained networks (e.g., via stable rank of activation matrices at each layer) would complete the quantitative test of Equation . On the applied side, measuring inference latency, energy, and peak RAM on Cortex-M4/M7 hardware would connect scaling behavior to the deployment metrics that practitioners actually optimize for.

assessments.rationale: The illustrative comparison uses a 5-layer LeNet and 110-layer ResNet under the same CIFAR-100 task, but the paper explicitly states that it cannot claim causality and discusses capacity and regularization as associated factors.
The evidence reports ECE, MCE, NLL, and reliability diagrams, but explicitly notes that MCE is highly sensitive to binning and less suited to small test sets, leaving measurement-validity concerns.

The table reports temperature-scaling results across multiple vision and NLP datasets and architectures, indicating effectiveness in several tested settings, though not broad validity beyond those experiments.
The survey confirms that LeNet and ResNet differ substantially in depth, architecture, and historical generation, reinforcing the comparison-fairness concern.

result.next_focus: Find controlled same-architecture and same-training comparisons, validation of calibration metrics against probabilistic correctness, and evidence for temperature scaling across broader domains and model families.

result.weak_point: 시대 효과를 주장하면서 LeNet과 ResNet처럼 깊이·구조·학습 절차가 크게 다른 모델을 비교해, 관찰된 보정 차이를 ‘현대성’ 자체의 효과로 분리하지 못한다.

attack_questions.question: LeNet과 ResNet의 차이에서 구조, 깊이, 정규화, 학습 절차의 영향을 어떻게 분리했는가?
사용한 보정 지표가 실제 확률적 신뢰도 부족과 지표·binning·평가 설계의 artifacts를 어떻게 구별하는가?
temperature scaling의 효과를 평가된 특정 구조와 vision·NLP 과제 밖으로 일반화할 근거는 무엇인가?

qualifies.basis: CIFAR-100에서 5-layer LeNet과 110-layer ResNet의 reliability diagram 비교, 여러 구조·vision/NLP 데이터셋의 calibration 결과 및 temperature scaling 표를 제공한다. 다만 저자도 인과성을 주장할 수 없다고 명시하며 MCE의 binning 민감성을 지적한다.

unresolved.basis: 제시된 청크는 OOD 탐지의 학습 설정을 설명하지만, 본 주장인 시대별 calibration 차이나 temperature scaling 효과를 직접 검증하지 않는다.

defensible_scope.claim: 평가된 특정 vision·NLP 데이터셋과 모델 설정에서, 일부 현대 신경망은 선택된 구형 모델보다 덜 보정되었고 temperature scaling은 여러 설정에서 효과를 보였다.
conditions: 비교 대상이 특정 LeNet·ResNet 및 논문이 평가한 모델·과제로 한정된다.
calibration은 논문에서 사용한 ECE, MCE, NLL 및 reliability diagram 기준으로 해석한다.
temperature scaling의 효과는 평가된 설정에서만 주장한다.
excluded_scope: 모든 현대 신경망과 모든 구형 신경망
calibration 차이가 모델 시대 자체의 인과 효과라는 주장
평가되지 않은 도메인·모델·데이터셋에서 temperature scaling이 일반적으로 효과적이라는 주장

assumption_impacts.impact: 주장은 시대 간 일반 비교가 아니라 특정 모델 구성 간 비교로 좁아진다.
주장은 사용된 calibration 지표와 평가 설계가 타당하다는 조건부 결과로 좁아진다.
주장은 선택된 LeNet 및 역사적 baseline에 대한 결과로 좁아진다.
temperature scaling의 효과 주장은 논문에서 평가한 모델과 과제로 제한된다.

limitations: 비교 설계가 architecture, depth, training procedure를 완전히 통제하지 않는다.
MCE는 binning과 작은 test set에 민감하다.
제시된 외부 자료는 본 주장을 직접 반박하거나 독립적으로 확증하지 않는다.

findings.detail: ev_2 cites an architecture survey, but its supplied chunk is a passage from the calibration paper describing LeNet and ResNet reliability diagrams. The chunk therefore does not ground the cited survey source or its rationale that the survey confirms the comparison differences.
